items.title: From Closed-Set Annotation to In-Context Discovery: Biologically Grounded LLMs for Cellular Profiling
items.abstract_or_text: Tumour heterogeneity reflects both cellular identity (lineage) and state (active transcriptional programs), yet computational methods generally analyse these axes separately. We introduce CellScribe, a generative framework that conditions a pretrained language model on frozen single cell foundation model embeddings through AdaLN adapters, enabling one shared model to generate an ontology- grounded cell type or a quantified meta-program profile. Supervised multitask fine- tuning produces fine grained typing across hundreds of cell types and outperforms generative and retrieval baselines on meta-program identification under study-holdout evaluation. We further train the model with reinforcement learning, scoring its generations against cell ontology distance and meta-program agreement, so that they align with biological knowledge rather than token agreement. To identify new cell types not present in the supervised training data, we post-train the model to read several labelled example cells in a single context, each conditioning its own text span, and infer the type of a query cell through in-context learning. CellScribe thus unifies cell identity and state in one generative interface, grounds both in biological structure, and identifies cell types outside the supervised vocabulary.

items.title: Human-Guided Agentic AI for End-to-End EHR Research: Sequential Antibody-Drug Conjugate Pathways in Breast Cancer
items.abstract_or_text: PURPOSE: To demonstrate an end-to-end research workflow combining a large electronic health record (EHR) resource and a multi-agent artificial intelligence (AI) system governed by Human-Guided Orchestration (HGO), using sequential sacituzumab govitecan (SG) and trastuzumab deruxtecan (T-DXd) orders in breast cancer as the clinical use case. METHODS: A June 2026 EHR release contained 4.95 million patients, including 156,051 with breast cancer codes. Muse Spark supported cohort construction, executable statistical analysis, data-quality checks, literature retrieval, and reporting executed through Symbiotic Agent Teaming (SAT) under investigator direction. The main clinical measure was the second-drug record span, from first to last order. Analyses were descriptive and unadjusted; orders did not confirm administration or progression. RESULTS: The workflow identified 106 patients: 73 had T-DXd ordered first and 33 had SG ordered first. Median second-drug spans were 63 days (interquartile range [IQR], 29-116) for SG after T-DXd and 49 days (IQR, 21-126) for T-DXd after SG; the median difference was -14 days (95% bootstrap CI, -41 to 21; distributional P = 0.42). Reported outputs additionally included cohort definitions, aggregate analyses, evidence context, figures, and a preliminary draft manuscript. CONCLUSION: This study provides a concrete model for integrating large EHR resources, agentic AI, and human expertise across the research cycle. The ADC use case illustrates how computational execution and Expert-in-the-Loop (EITL) adjudication can produce interpretable research outputs and refine their scientific meaning, providing a foundation for extending and evaluating this approach across clinical questions.

items.title: Beyond ICD Codes: Semantic IDs for Generative Medical Coding
items.abstract_or_text: Generative approaches to automatic International Classification of Diseases (ICD) coding use large language models (LLMs) to predict ICD codes from clinical documents. However, original ICD code strings are not ideal generation targets because the ICD hierarchy does not always reflect clinical relationships, and LLMs struggle to interpret and generate these codes. We introduce SemICD, a framework that trains LLMs to generate Semantic IDs (SIDs) instead. SemICD constructs SIDs by hierarchically clustering embeddings of textual code profiles, allowing semantically related codes to share prefixes while each complete SID uniquely identifies one ICD code. To align the SID tokens with clinical semantics, we employ two auxiliary tasks for bidirectional generation between textual code profiles and SIDs. Experiments on MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV with four LLMs show that SemICD outperforms direct code generation, improving Micro-F1 by 1.34-8.00 points. Our code is available at https://github.com/youwillbethebest/SemICD.

items.title: Quantifying Cancer Clinical Trial Eligibility Using Artificial Intelligence-Based Matching
items.abstract_or_text: PURPOSE: To develop and validate an artificial intelligence-enabled platform that combines efficient screening with explicit eligibility logic by converting unstructured cancer trial criteria into reusable structured queries, and illustrates potential eligibility using synthetic patients. METHODS: We downloaded actively recruiting US interventional treatment trials for advanced/metastatic breast cancer, colon cancer, and non-small cell lung cancer from ClinicalTrials.gov. Medical oncologists created 24 synthetic patient vignettes. A large language model converted trial eligibility criteria into Structured Query Language (SQL) code and patient information into structured records, enabling rule-based matching without further LLM inference. Cancer details and treatment history were considered, but not laboratory results or comorbidities. Validation included physician editing of generated eligibility code for 30 trials and independent assessments by two physicians, followed by consensus adjudication, for eligibility across ten trials. We descriptively summarized potential eligibility by trial characteristics and when varying age, ECOG performance status, sex, and ZIP code. RESULTS: Of 833 candidate trials, 746 met inclusion criteria. Performing matching for all 746 trials took a median of 0.459 seconds per patient, excluding patient-data preparation. Against physician consensus, automated matching agreed on 230/240 patient-trial pairs (95.8%; sensitivity 83.3%, specificity 100%). Across synthetic patients, potentially eligible trials ranged from 10 to 258 without geographic restrictions. Counts decreased with worse performance status and geographic restriction and were relatively stable across ages 30-90. Later-phase, randomized, and molecularly selective trials generally matched fewer vignettes. CONCLUSION: LLM-generated SQL enables rapid, explicit rule-based screening for potential trial eligibility. Evaluation in synthetic vignettes supports feasibility, while missed matches underscore the need for further validation.

items.title: ReproBAIT: Can coding agents build their own biological AI tools?
items.abstract_or_text: Large language models are increasingly competent at leveraging scientific knowledge and existing computational tools to execute complex workflows. At present, little information exists on their ability to reconstruct tools when given limited descriptions of such tools. We introduce an evaluation titled ReproBAIT (Reproducing Biological AI Tools), which measures the ability of coding agents to design, implement, and train biological AI tools taken from published research across a range of information access conditions. The coding agent is securely sandboxed without internet access and receives training data, a fixed time and compute budget, and limited information about the tool to replicate. We then score the reproduced biological AI tool based on its performance (tool-specific metrics) on held-out data. We evaluated a set of biological AI tools of varying complexities: ProteinMPNN, an inverse protein folding tool, RFdiffusion3, an all-atom generative diffusion tool, and a closed-source molecular design tool. We institute a methodology to check for memorisation, as the open source tools are likely to be included in models' pretraining corpus. Across a range of leading closed- and open-source coding agents, we find substantial reproduction capability for some selected tools, though limited capability for a highly complex tool. We find moderate evidence consistent with memorisation, varying across coding agents. These results suggest that tool developers need to be increasingly cautious when releasing information about the tools publicly; re-creation of the tool based on such information could undermine a tool's commercial value or invalidate dual-use managed access strategies.

items.title: Titan-Llama: Retrofitting Pre-trained LLMs with External Neural Memory Modules
items.abstract_or_text: Transformers are efficient to pre-train at scale because attention permits parallel computation across sequence positions, but long-context inference requires increasingly large KV caches. Efficient recurrent alternatives reduce the asymptotic complexity of inference, but their sequential dependence limits token-wise parallelism during training, making them harder to scale. Further, the current paradigm of extending long context tasks creates competing notions of retaining information precisely and keeping long-context inference efficient. To address this gap, we introduce Titan-Llama, a post-training method for retrofitting attention-based language models with a hierarchical memory architecture that updates parameters at test-time. Titan-Llama applies a blockwise attention mask and preserves full-fidelity attention over recent tokens while compressing historical context into recurrent, fixed-size neural memory modules (NMMs). Our formulation allows pre-trained attention layers to be replaced without training a new language model from scratch. On Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct, Titan-Llama raises accuracy over segmented attention windows from 23.87\% to 40.51\% on QuALITY and from 14.50\% to 40.75\% on LongHealth. Inference benchmarks show more than 20\% faster prefill, 37\% faster decode at medium context lengths, and 24\% lower steady-state decode memory usage in the evaluated configurations. Together, these results demonstrate that incorporating memory architecture mechanisms that utilize test-time training effectively modulates long-context behavior of pre-trained models, offering a practical route to adapting pre-trained transformers for efficient long-context inference. Our code is released on Github https://github.com/sarahpannn/titans-pytorch/tree/main{GitHub}

items.title: Physics-Informed Deep Learning in Oncology
items.abstract_or_text: Deep learning has enabled substantial advances in oncology, including cancer detection and diagnosis, medical image analysis, tumor characterization, treatment planning, response assessment, and outcome prediction. However, conventional data-driven models often require large annotated datasets, exhibit limited generalization across heterogeneous clinical settings, and lack explicit mechanisms for incorporating the physical, physiological, and biological principles underlying cancer development and treatment. Physics-informed deep learning (PIDL) integrates governing physical laws, mechanistic models, physiological constraints, and domain knowledge into deep learning frameworks, providing a principled approach for learning from sparse, noisy, and heterogeneous oncological data. This review presents a task-oriented synthesis of PIDL methods across oncology, encompassing neural networks, Kolmogorov-Arnold networks, convolutional and vision architectures, neural operators, generative models, and hybrid physics-data-driven frameworks. Their applications are examined across cancer detection and diagnosis, image reconstruction and analysis, tumor characterization, quantitative imaging, tumor progression, treatment response, radiation therapy, treatment planning, and multimodal clinical modeling. Based on the synthesized methodological and application-level evidence, we develop task-optimized PIDL workflows that align the clinical task with appropriate data representations, physical constraints, model architectures, and validation strategies. We further analyze key challenges, including physical-model fidelity, computational scalability, uncertainty quantification, domain generalization, standardized benchmarking, and clinical validation.

items.title: Feasibility and Measurement Properties of a Large Language Model-Based Virtual Patient Laboratory for Clinical Reasoning Training in Physical Therapy Students: Single-Arm Pilot Study
items.abstract_or_text: Background: Large language models (LLMs) configured as virtual patients may expand structured practice of clinical reasoning in health professions education. Before testing effectiveness, it must be established whether students engage with them and whether the resulting scores are complete, reliable, and related to performance with real patients. Our earlier pilot randomized trial found very low engagement with a less structured LLM-based approach. Objective: This study aimed to assess the feasibility (adherence, acceptability, and data completeness) of a revised, structured LLM-based clinical reasoning laboratory (Laboratorio de Inteligencia Artificial [LIA]) in undergraduate physical therapy education and to explore its measurement properties, including its association with clinical judgment with a real patient assessed with the Lasater Clinical Judgment Rubric (LCJR). Methods: In this single-arm pilot feasibility study, 27 third-year physical therapy students at a Spanish university completed, in 2024-2025, 3 virtual patient cases (lumbar, cervical, and thoracic spine pain) simulated by ChatGPT (GPT-4) over 4 weeks, each twice. ChatGPT scored each attempt from 0 to 4 on the same 10 dimensions of the Lasater Clinical Judgment Rubric (LCJR; 0-40 points) that human assessors applied (1-4 per dimension; 10-40 points) during a real patient encounter. Feasibility outcomes were case completion, data completeness, and satisfaction (0-10). Measurement outcomes were internal consistency and convergent validity (Spearman correlations between model-generated and human LCJR scores). Variability estimates informed the sample size of a future trial. Results: All 27 students were assessed with the LCJR; 22 (81%) completed at least 1 LIA case. Both attempts of the lumbar, cervical, and thoracic cases were completed by 78%, 63%, and 74% of students, respectively. Satisfaction data were available for 15 students (56%; mean 6.0, SD 1.3), and missing secondary data clustered in the third rotation. Internal consistency was excellent for the LCJR (alpha=.96) and ranged from .43 to .90 for model-generated ratings. Model-generated LIA scores clustered near the maximum (mean 36.0, SD 1.4). Among completers, LIA scores correlated weakly with the LCJR (rho=0.25, 95% CI -0.20 to 0.61; rho=0.44, 95% CI 0.05-0.71, when noncompleted attempts were scored as 0). Grade point average correlated almost perfectly with the LCJR (rho=0.96; n=22); after adjustment for it, the LIA-LCJR association disappeared (partial rho=-0.10). A future trial would require approximately 39 students per group (80% power, conservative variance). Conclusions: Delivering the LIA within the curriculum was feasible, but clinical judgment ratings generated by ChatGPT did not reflect those of human assessors with a real patient: they clustered near the maximum and showed no convergent validity once noncompletion was separated from performance. LLM-generated ratings should not be used as outcome or assessment measures without validation against human raters. Case calibration, completion tracking, and clarification of the GPA-LCJR relationship are also needed before a definitive trial. Trial Registration: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT06809634; https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06809634

items.title: PAINT: A Framework for Multilingual Pain Representation from Medical Licensing Exams to Real-World Clinical Texts
items.abstract_or_text: Pain is one of the most common and clinically important symptoms, reflecting disease onset, progression, and treatment response. However, pain is difficult to accurately capture and interpret from medical text, as its expression varies across languages, documentation types, and patient demographics, and is often embedded in terminology, negation, temporality, and contextual descriptions. Existing pain-related studies remain largely monolingual or limited to narrow clinical settings. In this study, we introduce PAINT, a multilingual framework for studying pain representation across medical exams and real-world clinical texts. PAINT includes nine pain-focused dataset partitions spanning English, Spanish, Portuguese, and Japanese, with clinician annotations in all four languages. We curated a structured schema covering pain relevance, pain presence, anatomical location, pain descriptors, and demographic information. To capture multilingual pain representations, we leverage large language models (LLMs) and adopt an ensemble strategy to improve performance. Ten clinicians across four languages validate the labels: the ensemble reaches macro-F1 of 0.91-1.00 on pain relevance and pain presence and 92-100% accuracy on demographics, with inter-annotator κ of 0.82-1.00. We release the WorldMedQA-Pain ensemble labels, the extraction pipeline, validation scripts, and clinician annotation sheets for publicly licensed corpora, providing a foundation for pain-centered clinical NLP and for studying pain documentation across languages and healthcare contexts.

items.title: PRISMATIC : Prescription Risk Inspection System for Multi-Agent Treatment Interaction in Clinical Decision-Making
items.abstract_or_text: Medical prescribing errors for multimorbid patients, who require complex drug regimens, are a major patient safety concern. These errors often stem from fragmented decision-making across medical specialties, a critical coordination failure that leads to adverse drug events and rehospitalizations. To address this coordination challenge, we introduce PRISMATIC, a multi-agent architecture where specialized agents, each representing a workflow role, collaboratively generate and refine treatment plans. Operating on a blackboard architecture, the system first structures patient information from clinical notes, then iteratively develops safe, rational, and interpretable drug regimens. The agents' collaboration is governed by two novel adaptive coordination mechanisms: (1) Dynamic Self-Updating Weight Adjustment (DSWA), a long-term mechanism that adjusts the influence weights of agents based on historical case outcomes, enabling the system to adapt and trust more reliable specialists over time. (2) Discrepancy Feedback Precise Calibration (DFPC), a short-term mechanism where agents provide iterative feedback to resolve disagreements and eliminate prescription conflicts for the current patient. Experiments on patient records from the MIMIC-IV database show that PRISMATIC significantly reduces drug conflicts, improves prescription coverage, and enhances treatment consistency compared to strong LLM baselines. Our work demonstrates that structuring clinical co-treatment as a multi-agent coordination problem offers a promising path toward safer and more coherent multidisease management.

items.title: SVC: A Vision Transformer-based Spatially and Virtually Embedded Cell Model for Deciphering Subcellular Spatial Transcriptomic Heterogeneity
items.abstract_or_text: Subcellular transcript localization shapes gene regulation and cellular function, yet profiling it at scale remains difficult, limiting our ability to study subcellular heterogeneity across tissues and disease. Here, we present SVC, a Vision Transformer-based spatially and virtually embedded cell model that learns subcellular transcript organization within native tissue context directly from subcellular-resolution spatial transcriptomics. SVC represents each gene's subcellular localization as an image patch and uses other genes within the same cell as context, enabling subcellular contextual learning of spatial dependencies that govern intracellular organization. By integrating gene-function priors, cell morphology, spatial context, and, when available, cell identity, SVC captures unified, spatially grounded representations across genes and cells that connect subcellular organization to cellular state and tissue microenvironment. Across diverse subcellular-resolution spatial transcriptomics datasets, SVC accurately predicts cell-specific subcellular transcript localization and co-organization, generalizes across tissues and technical platforms, and supports subcellular imputation of unmeasured genes and in silico perturbation. Leveraging these capabilities, SVC highlights disease-associated patterns of intracellular transcript reorganization and spatially heterogeneous responses to gene perturbations. Beyond prediction, SVC reveals systematic variation in subcellular transcript organization associated with gene function, cellular states, and tissue microenvironments, uncovering de novo spatial biology that is not accessible by cell-level analysis. SVC's learned representations further transfer to cell- and tissue-level tasks, including cell-level expression imputation, cell clustering, and spatial domain detection. Together, SVC provides a general framework for modeling and interrogating subcellular transcript organization in situ, enabling scalable discovery of subcellular spatial biology.

items.title: Detection of Potato Plant Leaf Diseases using Convolutional Neural Networks
items.abstract_or_text: Potato is an important food-security crop in Ethiopia, but its production is affected by foliar diseases, particularly early blight and late blight. This study develops a lightweight convolutional neural network (CNN) to classify potato leaves into three categories: healthy, early blight, and late blight. The proposed model was trained using 2,215 images from the PlantVillage dataset and evaluated on an independent field dataset containing 247 images collected from potato farms in Banja, Awi Zone, Ethiopia. On PlantVillage, the model achieved 99.04% training accuracy, 98.21% validation accuracy, and 98.66% test accuracy. On the field dataset, it achieved 90.28% accuracy. The study also compares the proposed CNN with VGG16 and MobileNetV2 in terms of classification performance and computational efficiency. The proposed model contains 446,787 trainable parameters, occupies approximately 1.70 MB, and requires an average of 5.58 seconds per training epoch in the reported experimental setup, compared with 9.96 seconds for VGG16 and 7.68 seconds for MobileNetV2. The results demonstrate the potential of a compact CNN for potato leaf disease classification and highlight the importance of independent field evaluation, where image conditions are more variable than in controlled benchmark datasets. The proposed approach may support preliminary disease identification for smallholder farmers in Ethiopia and similar agricultural settings.

items.title: Cerebrospinal fluid dopa-decarboxylase is a biomarker of dopaminergic dysfunction
items.abstract_or_text: Background. Nigrostriatal dopaminergic dysfunction, a biological anchor of Parkinson's disease (PD), is routinely assessed using single-photon emission computed tomography of the dopamine transporter (DaT-SPECT). Dopa decarboxylase (DDC) in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) is a promising biomarker of dopaminergic dysfunction, but its association with DaT-SPECT has to be demonstrated. Objectives. To investigate the association of CSF DDC with DaT-SPECT. Methods. We first analysed proteomic and DaT-SPECT data from the Parkinson's Progression Markers Initiative (PPMI), including PD (n=891), prodromal PD (n=867) and healthy controls (n=161). We then verified this association in a single-center clinical cohort (UNIPG), including PD/Dementia with Lewy Bodies (DLB) (n=78), atypical parkinsonisms (AP, n=11), other neurodegenerative diseases (OND, n=25) and controls (CTRL, n=40). Here, CSF DDC was measured by a novel fully automated quantitative immunoassay. Results. In PPMI, among 129 proteins assessed, DDC showed the strongest association with DaT-SPECT ({beta} = -0.132, FDR = 6.92 x 10-33). Across PPMI and UNIPG cohorts, DDC correlated with striatal binding ratio (SBR) ({rho} = -0.377, P < 0.001; {rho} = -0.466, P < 0.001, respectively) and accurately discriminated positive from negative scans (AUC 0.811, 95% CI 0.762-0.859; AUC 0.870, 95% CI 0.777-0.963, respectively). In PPMI prodromal cases, higher DDC predicted faster motor progression. In UNIPG, DDC distinguished PD/DLB and AP from OND and CTRL groups (AUC 0.830, 95% CI 0.764-0.896), independently of dopaminergic treatment. Conclusion. CSF DDC reflects nigrostriatal dopaminergic dysfunction, representing a potential quantitative biochemical alternative to DaT-SPECT that might be readily implemented via automated immunoassays.

items.title: ProtModernBERT: Compute-Efficient Protein Language Modeling
items.abstract_or_text: Large protein language models provide a powerful framework for learning sequence-function relationships and guiding experimental design. However, architectural improvements are underexplored, especially in low-compute regimes of relevance for resource-constrained research laboratories. We show that the training cost for encoder-only transformer architectures can be reduced by leveraging modern architectural refinements, offering an encouraging performance / compute-efficiency trade-off. We introduce ProtModernBERT, a modernized BERT-style model pre-trained on amino acid sequences, and compare it with ProtBert, Amplify, and ESM2 across a set of supervised structural tasks -encompassing secondary structure prediction, disorder prediction, and subcellular localization- and ProteinGym's zero-shot functional benchmark. We find that ProtModernBERT matches or closely tracks the performance of Amplify-120M and ProtBert with up to 80-90\% reduction in pre-training FLOPs, and narrows the gap to ESM2 when controlling for pre-training. Our analysis using a cluster-based validation protocol for hyperparameter selection and randomly initialized models disentangles the contributions of architecture and data, showing that modern components provide stronger inductive biases that are more consequential than parameter count in low-compute regimes.

items.title: Serum proteins predict incident inflammatory bowel disease 14 years before diagnosis: a machine-learning and Cox modelling in the UK Biobank
items.abstract_or_text: Using an analysis pipeline that combines machine learning-based feature selection with classical statistical modelling, we aimed to predict incident inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) and to identify candidate proteins associated with disease development. We used UK Biobank data in an observational cohort study of 52,331 participants with proteomics data and without a history of IBD. The cohort was split into an 80/20 train/test dataset, and three separate extreme gradient boosting models were trained on the training dataset. Using Shapley values, we ranked the predictive importance of 2,912 proteins for incident IBD, Crohn's disease (CD), and ulcerative colitis (UC). The top 20 proteins per outcome served as features in multivariate Cox models predicting 350 incident cases over 14 years. All three proteomics Cox models showed moderate discrimination in the test dataset, with the UC model performing the best (C-index: 0.68), followed by IBD (C-index: 0.65), and CD (C-index: 0.60). All proteomics models outperformed clinical models. Smoking remained the only significant clinical predictor in the combined proteomics + clinical model. 48 unique proteins were identified across the three models, with 16 reaching statistical significance (p< 0.05). Machine learning-based feature selection with statistical survival modelling identifies plasma proteins that predict incident IBD and highlight biologically plausible, potentially targetable pathways in the preclinical phase of IBD.

items.title: MRI Biomarkers for Brain Metastases in Lung Cancer Using Machine Learning
items.abstract_or_text: Purpose: Existing prognostic models for brain metastases from lung cancer rely on clinical variables and do not capture the biological heterogeneity of host or tumor factors underlying survival outcomes. We evaluated whether MRI-derived radiomic biomarkers improve prognostic stratification beyond clinical variables. We also investigated their biological correlates using matched histopathology. Experimental Design: This retrospective study included 103 patients with brain metastases from lung cancer and matched pre-operative MRI and histopathology. Radiomic features from T1-weighted contrast-enhanced and T2-weighted fluid-attenuated inversion recovery sequences were combined with clinical variables to train Cox proportional hazards, random survival forest, and DeepSurv models for overall survival (OS), CNS progression, and leptomeningeal (LM) progression. Risk groups from an imaging-only model were compared for clinical and histopathologic differences. Results: Imaging features improved prognostic performance beyond clinical variables across all modeling frameworks, with the combined clinical-imaging DeepSurv model achieving the highest concordance index for OS (0.728). Risk groups from the best-performing model for each endpoint differed significantly in OS (median 26.7 vs. 9.1 months, p < 0.001) and LM progression (p = 0.003), but not in CNS progression. Imaging-only risk groups did not differ significantly in any clinical variable, but high-risk patients were less likely to have tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (46% vs. 77%, p = 0.010) and PD-L1 expression [≥] 50% (10% vs. 32%, p = 0.049). Conclusions: MRI radiomic biomarkers provide prognostic information beyond established clinical variables in lung cancer brain metastases and correspond to features of the tumor immune microenvironment, supporting their potential to refine risk stratification.

items.title: HEM-Med: A Hierarchical Agentic Memory Framework for Safe Multi-Center Medication Recommendation
items.abstract_or_text: Medication recommendation (MR) is critical for clinical decision support. While existing MR methods are mostly designed for single-center learning, where only one independent hospital is involved, multi-center MR with hospitals of different scales has become increasingly demanding in practice. In multi center settings, abundant data from large medical centers can improve recommendation performance for low-resource centers. Despite a few preliminary attempts on this task, two critical gaps remain. Gap 1: Existing multi-center methods fail to disentangle transferable cross-hospital clinical experience from hospital-specific prescribing patterns, limiting clinical feasibility and physician acceptance. Gap 2: They commonly overlook multi label safety constraints of MR, including drug-drug interaction risks and local formulary feasibility, which are essential for safe real-world deployment. To address these gaps, we propose HEM-Med, a novel hierarchical agentic memory framework for multi-center MR. To address Gap 1, we design a disentangled hierarchical memory module that builds patient-level medication context attribution records and disentangles them into cross hospital experience memory and hospital-specific residual memory. To address Gap 2, we introduce a safety-aware medication set generation module, which integrates dual-level experience retrieval with safety-aware set decoding to produce clinically relevant, safer, and locally adaptive medication recommendations. Experiments on a real-world multi-center eICU dataset show that HEM-Med outperforms representative transfer learning, LLM-based, and MR baselines in terms of both recommendation accuracy and safety.

items.title: Learning When to Trust Medical Knowledge: Regression-Safe Routing for Clinical Reasoning
items.abstract_or_text: Clinical reasoning LLMs need external medical knowledge, but retrieved evidence and reasoning chains can be outdated, poisoned, or hallucinated. Harmful knowledge can cause regression: changing a correct answer into an incorrect one. We construct a medical knowledge-poisoning benchmark covering retrieved evidence and reasoning chains, with seven attack families filtered by a three-judge "subtle-but-wrong" vote and paired clean exams that separate poisoning effects from question difficulty. No fixed knowledge-use strategy is robust across these settings: strong RAG methods trade robustness to poisoned evidence against accuracy when evidence is useful. We formulate knowledge use as per-instance routing and introduce Med-TrustRouter, a lightweight controller that keeps the solver frozen. From leakage-free runtime signals, it estimates each action's expected correctness gain and uncertainty, preserving the base answer unless another action is confidently better. Across seven medical reasoning settings, Med-TrustRouter achieves 78.9 macro and 69.2 worst-case accuracy, matching the strongest competitor on macro accuracy while substantially improving the worst-case floor. Its gains transfer across solvers and evidence judges, unlike a hand-coded router using the same signals. Similar performance across linear, tree, and neural action-value heads suggests that the benefit comes from routing rather than estimator complexity. These results support learning when to trust external knowledge for robust clinical reasoning.

items.title: DNA-LLM2Vec: Architecture-Aware Task-Conditioned Adaptation of Decoder DNA Foundation Models
items.abstract_or_text: Decoder DNA foundation models pretrain with dense next-token prediction and scale to long sequences, but their representations are directional. This is a poor fit for genomic tasks that need sequence context both upstream and downstream of a locus. Bidirectional masked-language-model encoders supply this context, but they pretrain more sparsely and scale less easily to long windows. We introduce DNA-LLM2Vec, a staged decoder-to-encoder framework that opens bidirectional context, repairs the resulting mismatch with masked next-token prediction, and applies contrastive views encoding strand and positional invariance. We instantiate it on two architecturally distinct backbones, DNAGPT and HyenaDNA, and evaluate seven biological task families (grouped from GB, NT, GUE, and GUE+EPI) with frozen linear probing. The benefits of conversion are architecture-aware and task-conditioned rather than uniform. Crop-based positional contrastive learning helps most for the extended-context families (enhancer-promoter interaction and Virus-COVID), raising frozen Avg-EPI MCC to 27.5% for DNAGPT and 26.7% for HyenaDNA, whereas for shorter, local families the results depend on backbone and tokenisation. Beyond classification, bidirectional context and MNTP improve causal-eQTL variant-effect prediction specifically at distance, and a base-pair mutagenesis diagnostic shows that adaptation organises motif-aware contact structure while reverse-complement training imprints strand-consistent geometry, yet neither predicts the best downstream view. DNA-LLM2Vec therefore produces frozen bidirectional representations whose most effective adaptation view depends on the task structure and the backbone. Code and checkpoints are available at https://github.com/semi-nothing/dna-llm2vec.

items.title: OmniScore: Universal Scoring of Diverse Biomolecular Complexes via Equivariant Geometry-Aware Discrete Representation Learning
items.abstract_or_text: Biomolecular structures provide a common physical basis for understanding molecular function and interactions. However, computational models typically specialize in individual molecular classes or tasks, hindering a unified representation of structural information across biological systems. Here we introduce OmniScore, a universal geometric encoder that learns shared representations of proteins, nucleic acids, small molecules and their complexes. Pretraining integrates geometric graph encoding, sequential modeling and tokenization with structural and physicochemical supervision. The frozen pretrained encoder supports complex-level model quality assessment and interaction prediction, as well as residue-level prediction, through task-specific heads. OmniScore outperforms the evaluated antibody--antigen quality-assessment baselines and also improves RNA structure ranking over baselines. For peptide-major histocompatibility complex interaction prediction, the OmniScore embeddings complement structure-prediction confidence metrics to improve predictive performance. Together, these findings support OmniScore as a shared geometric foundation for biomolecular representation and scoring across molecular classes and prediction scales, which may facilitate multi-component therapeutics development.

items.title: SkillScaffold: Scaffolding Agentic Reinforcement Learning with Policy-Adaptive Skill Credit Assignment and Selective Injection
items.abstract_or_text: Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) enables large language models (LLMs) to learn from multi-turn interactions with verifiable outcomes. Textual skills can improve exploration by distilling prior interactions into reusable guidance. However, existing skill-based RL approaches often either assume skill injection is beneficial or rely on indirect feedback or rollout-intensive evaluation to assess its utility. Our pilot studies show that rollout-based utility estimation for skill credit assignment is costly and unstable under limited sampling, while skill benefits vary across candidates and depend on the current policy's competence on each query. To address these challenges, we introduce SkillScaffold, a policy-adaptive training scaffold that combines low-cost skill-utility estimation with selective skill injection. By reusing outcome-verified training trajectories, SkillScaffold generates candidate skills and estimates their utility through outcome-aware likelihood comparisons, without candidate-specific environment rollouts. The resulting utility guides whether and which skill to inject, retaining skill-free execution when no candidate is estimated to help. Joint training enables the Generator to produce skills tailored to the evolving Executor. Scaffolded RL encourages skill internalization for skill-free inference. Experiments on ALFWorld, WebShop, ScienceWorld, and τ^2-Bench demonstrate gains over strong agentic-RL and skill-based RL baselines across both short- and long-horizon tasks. Ablations and further analyses support the importance of utility-based selection and abstention. Our code is available at https://github.com/Vaidurya00/SkillScaffold.

items.title: Benchmarking Self-Supervised 3D Medical Vision Foundation Models and Transferability Estimation
items.abstract_or_text: Self-supervised pretraining has expanded the pool of 3D medical foundation models, but published evaluations use different datasets, endpoints and fine-tuning protocols. Models also differ in architecture, pretraining objective and data, while downstream targets range from voxel-level masks to patient-level diagnoses and outcomes. As a result, published findings provide little directly comparable evidence for choosing a model for a new task. Direct comparison of adaptation performance requires fine-tuning candidates on labelled target data, at substantial computational cost. We benchmark 23 candidates across the same 14 segmentation, classification and regression tasks spanning multiple anatomies and modalities. No candidate ranked among the top three across all segmentation tasks or across all classification and regression tasks; a convolutional encoder could outperform a transformer trained with the same objective on one task but underperform it on another. We benchmark transferability estimators against the fine-tuned rankings and find that their agreement varies across dense segmentation, classification and regression. InsightRank uses task-appropriate frozen-feature statistics and architecture-aware pairwise comparisons to rank candidates before fine-tuning. Across the 23-model pool, mean Kendall tau-b was 0.431 for segmentation and 0.352 for classification and regression. The segmentation Top 3 contained a task winner on four of nine tasks; the image-level Top 3 contained none on the five tasks, despite better full-ranking agreement than the matched conventional estimators. A three-model shortlist reduced recorded extraction-plus-training job time by 85.8% across seven segmentation tasks. Together, the benchmark provides a common reference for model selection and InsightRank offers a lower-cost way to prioritize fine-tuning, with shortlist performance that differs by target type.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence-Based Modeling to Aid in the Identification of Genetic Conditions in Infants with Congenital Heart Disease
items.abstract_or_text: Background: Genetic conditions are common in congenital heart disease (CHD) and affect care, but are often missed or diagnosed late. We asked whether routine clinical data can shortlist the most likely genetic conditions. Methods: Retrospective single-center cohort of children with CHD and an echocardiogram who had either a confirmed genetic diagnosis or negative cytogenetic testing and CHD gene sequencing. Echocardiogram images and serial medical record data were added as model inputs in the order they become clinically available. Class balanced logistic regression (LR) and a multimodal deep learning fusion network were fitted to the same inputs at each step. The primary metric was balanced top-3 accuracy (correct diagnosis among the top three, averaged across conditions), with bootstrap intervals. Results: The cohort included 1,720 children (988 with common CHD-associated genetic conditions, 231 rare diagnoses, 501 negative testing). Using only inputs generated at the echocardiogram visit, LR reached a balanced top-3 accuracy 0.758 (chance 0.429). Serial records, radiology notes and ICD-10 codes, raised this to 0.809. Multimodal fusion performed similarly at each stage. With a genetic condition withheld from training, the fusion embedding placed affected children nearest to others sharing a gene group in 0.37 of cases versus 0.10 without the embedding (+0.268 [95% CI +0.242, +0.295]). Conclusions: Routine clinical data available at first echocardiogram can help identify likely genetic diagnoses, and later coded inputs ceiling. Multimodal fusion added no accuracy over LR, but places children sharing a genetic cause near one another, making nearest-neighbor retrieval informative for undiagnosed children.

items.title: Constructed Negatives Shape the Evaluation of Sequence-Based Protein--Protein Interaction Models
items.abstract_or_text: Many machine-learning tasks, including representation learning, rely on negative examples that are constructed rather than directly observed. This issue is especially important for protein--protein interaction (PPI) prediction, where experimentally established non-interactions are scarce. PPI models are therefore commonly trained and evaluated against sampled, unobserved protein pairs treated as negatives. We study how this construction affects model comparison. Keeping positives, protein-disjoint splits, class balance, and model selection fixed, we vary training and evaluation negatives independently across six constructions and four sequence-based models, three of which use protein language model (pLM) representations. Changing only the test negatives shifts AUPRC by up to 0.26, and the top-ranked architecture changes with the construction. Negatives matched to true partners in pLM representation space reduce all pLM-based models to near-chance performance, and shuffling partners within each class shows that the original pairing contributes little to AUROC. Constructed training negatives rarely outperform uniform sampling: on external data, they underperform it in 108 of 120 comparisons for the pLM-based models, with gains never exceeding 0.05 AUROC and losses up to 0.23. We release splits, negative-generation procedures, and evaluation code that allow training and evaluation negatives to be varied separately. Our results show that with constructed negatives, model comparisons are not just noisy but systematically sensitive to how negatives are defined, a methodological choice that is often left implicit.

items.title: EDIT-B Consortium: An External Pan-European Validation of an Innovative Machine Learning-Based Test for Bipolar Disorder Diagnosis
items.abstract_or_text: Background Differentiating bipolar disorder (BD) from major depressive disorder (MDD) during major depressive episodes remains a significant challenge. EDIT-B is an in vitro diagnostic test based on machine learning (ML) method integrating clinical metadata with adenosine-to-inosine (A-to-I) RNA editing signatures in eight genes (GAB2, IFNAR1, IL17RA, LYN, MDM2, PRKCB, PTPRC, ZNF267) to differentiate BD from MDD. Objective The objective of this study is to assess and confirm the diagnostic performance of EDIT-B in a new, independent, double-blind, external multicenter European cohort. Methods We evaluated EDIT-B results across four European centers (Spain, France, Denmark), compared to physician diagnoses. Explainability and sensitivity analyses were performed to identify the primary drivers of the model. Findings In 393 patients with current major depressive episode (238 MDD; 155 BD), EDIT-B demonstrated robust performance: AUC-ROC of 0.873 (95%CI: 0.837-0.909); sensitivity of 82.6% (95%CI: 75.7-88.2%); and specificity of 80.3% (95%CI: 74.6-85.1%). Performances were consistent across sites and all stratified patient subgroups, corroborating previous results. Explainability analysis pointed RNA editing biomarkers as the most important variables for EDIT-B diagnosis. Conclusion This study confirms the diagnostic performances of EDIT-B showing that A-to-I RNA editing coupled with ML methods is a reliable approach to distinguish BD from MDD. Clinical implications EDIT-B represents an innovative, reliable, and complementary diagnostic tool supporting psychiatric practice and enhancing clinical outcomes with potential impact in reducing the diagnostic delays, tailoring the therapeutic strategy and improving therapeutic alliances. These findings may represent a significant advance toward precision psychiatry, with potential to reduce misdiagnosis and inappropriate treatment.

items.title: Calibration, Uncertainty, and Data Efficiency of Deep Learning Chest Radiograph Classifiers Under Cross-Dataset Distribution Shift: A Multi-Dataset Benchmark
items.abstract_or_text: Purpose To evaluate the external transportability of source-derived probability calibration for chest radiograph deep learning classifiers under distribution shift and determine its dependence on sample size and disease prevalence. Materials and Methods This retrospective secondary computational analysis of public, de-identified radiographic datasets involved no participant contact or new data collection. Cohort sizes were prespecified by availability without prospective power calculation: 106,686 NIH ChestX-ray14 images (29,323 patients; 1992-2015) for development and internal testing, 20,000 CheXpert images (20,000 patients; October 2002-July 2017), and 14,998 VinBigData images (2018-2020) for external testing. ResNet-18, DenseNet-121, and DeiT-Tiny classifiers for cardiomegaly and pleural effusion were trained across four patient fractions and three seeds (36 fits). Calibrators were fitted exclusively on NIH data. Twelve primary external Brier-score contrasts (temperature-scaled versus raw probabilities) were evaluated using paired cluster-bootstrapping with Holm adjustment. Results Temperature scaling reduced Brier scores in nine of 12 primary contrasts but worsened pleural effusion calibration on VinBigData across all architectures (Brier increases: ResNet-18, 0.001460 [95% CI: 0.001347, 0.001568]; DenseNet-121, 0.001193 [95% CI: 0.001109, 0.001274]; DeiT-Tiny, 0.000498 [95% CI: 0.000417, 0.000577]; all adjusted P=.006). Standardizing class weights to NIH prevalence reversed all CheXpert improvements. Although full versus 10% training improved external AUROC across all comparisons, DeiT-Tiny CheXpert pleural effusion Brier score worsened by 0.007039 despite a 0.032466 AUROC gain. At 80% selective image retention, calibrated ensembles retained only 12.3%-17.2% of VinBigData positive pleural effusion examinations. Conclusion Source-fitted calibration is not uniformly transportable across health systems, and discrimination gains do not guarantee calibrated probabilities. External evaluation must simultaneously assess probability reliability, prevalence shifts, and retained-case composition.

items.title: EpiGuard: An Autonomous Infectious-Disease Early Warning Agent Platform
items.abstract_or_text: Infectious disease outbreaks often spread rapidly before signs of widespread transmission become apparent, leaving a big challenge for rapid response and effective intervention. However, current infectious-disease early-warning systems face three major challenges: fragmented epidemiological evidence across diverse surveillance sources, highly uneven data availability across diseases and geographic regions, and delayed warning procedure caused by manual data collection, analysis, and reporting. To address these challenges, we present EpiGuard, an autonomous, continually self-improving agentic platform for timely and reliable early warning of more than 50 infectious diseases across different regions. EpiGuard proactively monitors and captures newly released official surveillance records, using the latest available evidence for risk assessments. It dynamically adjusts its analytical strategy across three evidence availability regimes, enabling reliable risk assessment under diverse data conditions, ranging from the absence of historical observations to sparse and abundant evidence. Moreover, EpiGuard learns from the successful execution process by preserving effective data-acquisition and analytical procedures as reusable standard operating procedures, enabling it to progressively generalize to previously unseen diseases and regions. We use officially released infectious-disease surveillance data from the China CDC and the United States CDC to evaluate EpiGuard's effectiveness. Experimental results demonstrate that EpiGuard outperforms state-of-the-art forecasting systems, improving forecasting performance by 9.68% and 14.04% on the China CDC and U.S. CDC datasets, respectively.

items.title: inLoRA-MINT: Internal Representations for Auditing Training Data in Domain-adapted LLMs
items.abstract_or_text: This work investigates the application of the Membership Inference Test (MINT) to large language models (LLMs) fine-tuned with LoRA, aiming to determine whether specific samples were used during training and address concerns about data privacy, leakage, and transparency. Building on our previous LoRA-MINT framework, which relies exclusively on perplexity under a strict black-box setting, we propose an approach based on intermediate model representations, including activations and parameter-dependent signals. These representations enable a MINT classifier to distinguish training from non-training samples without requiring full access to model parameters. We evaluated the method on four LLMs (Qwen, Phi-4, DeepSeek-V3, and LLaMA 3.2-3B) fine-tuned on three datasets covering medical, mathematical, and academic reasoning tasks. Results show consistent performance across architectures and domains, achieving scores between 95% and 98%, with robustness to variations in model configurations and data distributions. The proposed approach enables efficient auditing of sensitive training data and supports data provenance and compliance with emerging privacy and AI governance regulations. Although our experiments focus on LoRA-based fine-tuning, the methodology can be extended to other LLM adaptation techniques and, more broadly, to other AI models.

items.title: Cell Painting PLUS reveals phenotypic signatures for nephrotoxicity profiling in human RPTEC/TERT1
items.abstract_or_text: Multiplex high-throughput phenotypic profiling offers a cost-effective approach to monitor how chemical perturbations alter cellular morphology, thereby contributing to a mechanistic, human-centred hazard assessment with new approach methodologies in the context of Next Generation Risk Assessment (NGRA). In this study, we employed Cell Painting PLUS (CPP), an expanded high-content imaging assay that adds spatially resolved channels for mitochondria, lysosomes, actin, Golgi, RNA, DNA, and the endoplasmic reticulum, to renal RPTEC/TERT1 cells to evaluate nephrotoxicity. We profiled a set of nephrotoxic agents together with well-annotated reference chemicals encompassing diverse cellular targets to identify specific morphological profiles associated with distinct mechanisms of action (MoAs). Benchmark concentration modelling, correlation analysis, and hierarchical clustering of RPTEC/TERT1 CPP data captured specific morphological signatures of more than 300 tested compounds and enabled discrimination between closely related and opposing phenotypes. Comparison with CPP data generated in bone osteosarcoma U2OS cells highlighted cell-type-specific differences: despite lower overall activity, RPTEC/TERT1 resolved biologically relevant nephrotoxicity-associated phenotypes, highlighting the importance of using physiologically relevant cell models for contextspecific phenotypic profiling. Overall, these findings establish RPTEC-based CPP as a valuable phenotypic profiling platform supporting mechanistic nephrotoxicity assessment for integration into NGRA.

items.title: Personalised normative cardiac phenotyping reveals clinically relevant heterogeneity in cardiac shape and outcome risk
items.abstract_or_text: Standard cardiac biomarkers such as ejection fraction, ventricular volumes, and strain compress complex three-dimensional heart dynamics into a small set of predefined measurements, leaving clinically important heterogeneity unrecognised. Here we propose a personalised normative cardiac framework in which each individual is compared to a digital twin representing expected healthy cardiac function given their age, sex, and body habitus. We show that structured patterns of deviation from these normative twins, discovered through systematic exploration of a generative cardiac dynamics space, constitute novel dynamic phenotypes that are not captured by conventional biomarkers. Applied independently to two UK Biobank cardiac cohorts with distinct shape representation, a 128-dimensional four-chamber statistical shape descriptor (HeartSSM, n = 52,365) and a 64-dimensional deep generative latent space from a conditional variational mesh autoencoder (MeshHeart cVAE, n = up to 39,376), we identify reproducible, continuous deviation-from-normative-twin scores (three discrete deviation phenotypes in the HeartSSM cohort) that improve cardiovascular risk stratification beyond ejection fraction, ventricular volumes, myocardial mass, and strain. The strongest effect was seen for incident atrial fibrillation among individuals with preserved ejection fraction (at least 50%): incremental C-index delta C = +0.068 (5-fold cross-validated delta C = +0.063; likelihood-ratio P = 3.3 x 10^-8), with a separate, smaller effect for incident stroke in the same preserved-EF subgroup in the independent MeshHeart cVAE representation (which showed no signal for atrial fibrillation) (delta C = +0.024, P = 2.6 x 10^-4). Both effects were checked against placebo controls in which the deviation scores were replaced by Gaussian noise. To test whether the normative twin generalises beyond UK Biobank's specific scanning and processing pipeline, we applied the MeshHeart cVAE normative twin, unmodified, to an independent external cohort of healthy volunteers imaged at a different hospital (GenScan/Hammersmith, n = 315): deviation scores in this cohort were of comparable magnitude to the UK Biobank healthy reference (ratio of means = 1.09; Mann-Whitney P = 1.4 x 10^-5), indicating that the normative twin captures cross-site-transferable structure rather than a scanner- or pipeline-specific artefact. Our findings suggest that cardiac phenotyping can move beyond predefined measurements toward data-driven dynamic phenotypes that better capture the heterogeneity underlying cardiovascular disease risk, even among individuals whose ejection fraction appears normal.

items.title: Normative transcriptomic clues to thalamic developmental vulnerability in C9orf72-FTLD
items.abstract_or_text: C9orf72 encodes a protein that is important for both typical neurodevelopment and homeostatic processes across the lifespan. Pathogenic C9orf72 repeat expansions constitute the most common genetic cause of frontotemporal lobar degeneration (FTLD). Collectively, preclinical models and clinical neuroimaging studies have observed smaller thalamic volumes in C9orf72-associated FTLD, including in asymptomatic young adult C9orf72 repeat expansion carriers across 18 to 30 years old, supportive of potential neurodevelopmental origins. However, it is unknown whether asymptomatic young adult C9orf72 expansion carriers demonstrate volume differences in specific thalamic nuclei, as reported in older asymptomatic carriers and symptomatic patients; if so, normative transcriptomic patterns could reveal relevant neurodevelopmental and/or FTLD-related neurodegenerative processes. This study investigated volumetric MRI differences of the thalamic nuclei in asymptomatic young adult C9orf72 expansion carriers compared to non-carriers, and examined spatial associations with normative thalamic transcriptomics from 8 weeks post-conception through middle age. Young adult C9orf72 expansion carriers (n=72) and non-carriers (n=48) were enrolled in the Frontotemporal Dementia Prevention Initiative across Europe, Canada, and the USA (ages: 18-30 years; sex: 57% female). Spatial associations between young adult thalamic nuclei volumes and normative transcriptomics from the Allen Human Brain Atlas were examined using complementary data-driven and hypothesis-driven approaches. Spatial expression patterns of transcripts of interest were characterized across prenatal and postnatal neurodevelopment using BrainSpan data. Smaller volumes of the pulvinar, mediodorsal, and lateral nuclei were observed in young adult C9orf72 expansion carriers compared to non-carriers. These nuclei showed higher normative expression of transcripts involved concurrently in neurodevelopmental and C9orf72-associated FTLD neurodegenerative processes (including lysosomal, autophagic, and small GTPase functions), and lower normative expression of CALB1, a marker of prenatal human thalamic development. Normative expression of CALB2 (another human thalamic development marker) yielded positive correlations with C9orf72 across prenatal development to adulthood. These findings identify candidate transcripts that may provide insight into the molecular architecture leading to smaller thalamic nuclei volumes in C9orf72-associated FTLD.

items.title: PatientPheX: A Full-Text Biomedical Corpus for Patient-Specific Phenotype Information Extraction
items.abstract_or_text: Patient-specific phenotype information extraction identifiers and normalizes phenotype entities and links them with individual patients, supporting rare disease research and genotype-phenotype analysis. However, existing datasets rarely combine full-text biomedical content with detailed annotations of patients, phenotypes, related entities, and their associations. In this work, we present PatientPheX, a corpus for patient-specific phenotype information extraction comprising 200 full-text articles, primarily case reports and case series. The corpus provides mention annotations and normalization for seven biomedical entity types, together with explicit associations between patients and entities across sentences, paragraphs, and sections. Negated findings and composite phenotype mentions are also annotated. Corpus construction combines automated pre-annotation, large language model (LLM)-assisted verification, and manual review and adjudication. Benchmarks cover entity recognition and normalization and patient-phenotype association extraction using gold-standard and predicted entities. The overall document-level entity F1 was 86.95%, while phenotype F1 was 79.33%. The best relation extraction macro-F1 decreased from 84.14% with gold-standard entities to 54.98% with predicted entities, highlighting the combined challenges of phenotype extraction and patient attribution. PatientPheX provides a resource for developing and evaluating patient-centered information extraction methods and supports the construction of structured patient-level knowledge resources for phenotype-driven biomedical research.

items.title: Synaptic microRNA dysregulation orchestrates aberrant glutamatergic transmission in a human neuronal model of 22q11.2 deletion syndrome
items.abstract_or_text: 22q11.2 Deletion Syndrome (22q11DS), the most prevalent chromosomal microdeletion disorder in humans (incidence ~1 in 4,000 live births), arises from hemizygous deletions of a 1.5-3.0 Mb region on chromosome 22. Notably, 20-30% of individuals with 22q11DS develop schizophrenia (SCZ) by early adulthood, making 22q11DS one of the strongest genetic risk factors for SCZ. However, the mechanisms by which the 22q11.2 deletion perturbs neuronal function and drive psychotic manifestations in 22q11DS remain poorly defined. In this study, we generated human 2D cortical neurons and 3D cortical organoids from induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) derived from clinically well-characterized individuals with 22q11DS. Cellular and electrophysiological analyses revealed that 22q11DS neurons exhibit hyperexcitability, reduced glutamatergic synaptic transmission, and impaired homeostatic synaptic plasticity, which are pathophysiological hallmarks that may be relevant to the clinical, cognitive, and psychophysiological profiles of patients. Transcriptomic profiling of neurons and synaptosomes from 22q11DS cortical organoids uncovered dysregulated immune pathways and synaptic gene networks. Integrative mRNA-microRNA network analysis identified synergistic downregulation of hsa-miR-185-5p and hsa-miR-128-3p at synapses, driving aberrant regulation of immune and synaptic transcripts. Experimental knockdown of these microRNAs in control neurons recapitulated the molecular and functional phenotypes of 22q11DS neurons, thereby establishing a mechanistic link to synaptic dysfunction and impaired plasticity. Collectively, these findings delineate a multimodal mechanistic framework that bridges genetic vulnerability, synaptic pathology, and psychosis penetrance in 22q11DS, positioning dysregulated synaptic microRNAs as nodal regulators of neurodevelopmental networks and potential therapeutic targets.

items.title: HGRP: Heterogeneous Graph Neural Network for Routability Prediction
items.abstract_or_text: Routability prediction enables rapid evaluation of placement quality without routing, providing effective feedback for routability-driven placement optimization. Recent machine learning methods have achieved efficient routability prediction through data-driven approach. However, their prediction performance highly depends on the capability of input representations to capture essential circuit information. To address the limitations of existing circuit representations in simultaneously preserving logical topology, physical layout and routing resource information, this paper proposes HGRP, a heterogeneous graph neural network for routability prediction. HGRP models the cells, nets, and routing grids as distinct types of nodes and explicitly represents topological connectivity, spatial mapping, and grid adjacency, thereby constructing a heterogeneous graph representation that preserves multi-level circuit semantics. Based on the representation, a heterogeneous message passing mechanism is developed to enable information interaction and feature fusion among distinct types of nodes, effectively learning the complex correlations between circuit structures and routing behaviors. Experimental results on the CircuitNet dataset show that HGRP improves F1-score by 18.69\% relative improvements compared with the state-of-the-art in the congestion prediction task. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/ShenShan123/HGPR.

items.title: ForkGRPO: Efficient Exploration and Fine-Grained Credit Assignment for Diffusion Language Models
items.abstract_or_text: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) have advanced rapidly, yet strengthening their reasoning through reinforcement learning (RL) remains an open challenge. Any-order generation can suffer from entropy degradation, which narrows the reasoning paths available for exploration. Recent work mitigates this issue by applying standard GRPO with left-to-right generation. However, independently generating every rollout from the input prompt can leave alternative continuations from intermediate states underexplored, while trajectory-level advantages assign uniform credit to all tokens without distinguishing the contributions of individual reasoning segments. We propose ForkGRPO, an RL framework that couples efficient exploration with fine-grained segment-level credit assignment. It samples multiple continuations from high-entropy intermediate states along a reference trajectory, prioritizing textual boundaries and reusing shared prefixes. The continuations provide complementary learning signals: within-state group-relative advantages guide which continuations to reinforce, while Monte Carlo state-value differences indicate which reasoning segments improve expected outcomes. Among the evaluated architecture-preserving RL methods, ForkGRPO achieves the best performance on three of four benchmarks, while improving over the directly comparable JustGRPO by up to 1.2 percentage points and using up to 27.8% fewer generated tokens. ForkGRPO-Fast further achieves a 2.49\times training wall-clock speedup with negligible accuracy loss.

items.title: Generative design of functional disordered regions in a developmental transcription factor
items.abstract_or_text: Rapid advances in protein structure design have not translated to intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs). This is largely due to our incomplete understanding of how IDR sequence encodes function. Here, we use stem cell differentiation as a model to map functional sequence features in the IDR of transcription factor RUNX2. We show that RUNX2 requires its C-terminal IDR to bind chromatin and regulate gene expression during osteogenesis. Surprisingly, linear IDR sequence is dispensable, and instead features of the conformational ensemble predict function. We develop an algorithm for rational IDR design based on biophysical principles, and use it to generate functional IDRs de novo. Together, these results illustrate the central role for TF IDRs in chromatin binding and extend generative protein design beyond the folded proteome.

items.title: An Imaging Risk Score for Bipolar Disorder: Multimodal Comparison and Integration with Polygenic Risk
items.abstract_or_text: Background: Biological risk scores provide objective markers of bipolar disorder (BD) liability. Large-scale genome-wide association studies (GWASs) have led to polygenic risk scores (PRSs) that capture genetic liability to BD at the individual level. We lack a comparable large-scale effort to leverage a brain-wide association study (BWAS) to create an imaging risk score (IRS) that captures brain structural liability to BD at the individual-level. Here, we conduct the largest multivariate BWAS of BD and develop a BD IRS. We compare the BD IRS to the PRS and assess their combined predictive performance in multimodal risk score (MRS) models. Methods: Our multivariate BD BWAS used 153 structural neuroimaging features from 3902 cases and 6855 controls (mean age (sd)=35.47 years (13.42), 56.70% female) in a cross-validated machine learning approach. Using the resulting model coefficients, we constructed an IRS. We then evaluated the out-of-sample performance of the IRS, PRS derived from the largest GWAS to date, and combined MRS model using logistic regression in a subset of individuals with imaging and genetic data (nBD=486, ncontrols=1701, age (sd)=33.10 (12.02), 56.47% female). We also performed stratified analyses for demographic and BD clinical groups. Prediction performance was quantified using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). Subsequent analyses examined associations between each risk score and BD relevant symptoms in developing youth. Outcomes: In predicting case status, the BD BWAS model achieved a mean AUCBD of 0.62 (sdBD=0.08) and in stratified analyses, had higher prediction than subgroup-specific BWAS models. The BD type II BWAS was the only exception (AUCBDII=0.60, sdBDII=0.07 vs AUCBD=0.58, sdBD=0.09). The BD PRS had an AUCBD of 0.65 (CI95%=0.63-0.68) and a higher AUC than subtype-specific PRS in stratified analyses. The PRS typically attained a higher AUC than the IRS. Notably, the IRS and PRS were uncorrelated (r=0.03, p=0.11). MRS models outperformed the prediction of individual PRS and IRS with the strongest prediction for BD type I (AUCBD=0.74, CI95%=0.70-0.78). The IRS had the strongest associations with BD-related symptoms in developing youth including increased energy (OR=1.21, pfdr=0.03) and distress from psychotic-like experiences (OR=1.23, pfdr=0.04). Interpretation: Our BD IRS is a novel biological indicator of BD risk. The lack of correlation between the IRS and PRS along with improved MRS prediction suggests the two risk scores capture some orthogonal liability to BD. We show that integrating imaging and genetics is useful for biological characterization of BD and should be considered for the development of clinically relevant prediction models.

items.title: Brain Age Gap Progression in Individuals at Risk for Neurodegeneration
items.abstract_or_text: Neuroimaging is a widely used modality for characterizing neurodegeneration in various health conditions. Brain age gap has emerged as a promising biomarker for monitoring brain health from neuroimaging data using machine learning algorithms. Recent studies have leveraged coVariance neural networks (VNN)-driven pipelines based on the advancements in graph signal processing for relatively transparent construction of brain age gap from neuroimaging data. In this paper, we focus on a longitudinal study of VNN-based brain age gap in conjunction with Alzheimer's Progression Score (APS) in individuals that are at a higher risk of neurodegeneration due to family history of Alzheimer's disease. APS is a multimodal marker of disease progression. The longitudinal analysis of APS and VNN-derived brain age gap metrics revealed that a higher risk of disease progression at baseline predicted a larger rate of increase in brain age gap in follow-up visits. Thus, our findings revealed potential stratification in the brain age gap modulated by clinical/biological risks of AD in the at-risk population.

items.title: Flavins in Focus: Vitamin B2 as a Metabolic Keystone for Neuronal Repair in Regenerating Planarians
items.abstract_or_text: Regeneration imposes substantial metabolic demands to support the reconstruction of functional tissues. Essential vitamins are indispensable metabolic cofactors, yet whether their availability is spatially organized to support local metabolic demands within regenerative tissues remains largely unknown. Here, we identify previously undescribed flavin-rich cells, referred to as 'flavinocytes', that form an extensive network that spatially organizes vitamin B2 metabolism in the planarian Schmidtea mediterranea. Using endogenous flavin autofluorescence as a label-free in vivo metabolic readout, we show that this network consists of elongated cells that form longitudinal varicosity-containing strands closely associated with the central nervous system. RNAi-mediated disruption of riboflavin uptake and metabolism reduced flavin-associated autofluorescence and its spatial distribution within the animal, while affecting blastema formation, eye regeneration, and nervous system reconstruction. These findings demonstrate that riboflavin metabolism is required for successful regeneration. Single-cell transcriptomics, protein localization, and functional perturbations further suggest a reciprocal relationship between flavinocytes and the regenerating nervous system, pointing to coordinated neuro-metabolic interactions during tissue repair. Together, our findings demonstrate the importance of riboflavin metabolism for nervous system regeneration and provide new insight into the spatial organization of metabolism during tissue regeneration.

items.title: THE BILE ACID RECEPTOR TGR5 MODULATES HIPPOCAMPAL NEURAL STEM CELL STATE AND AGEING
items.abstract_or_text: Ageing locks hippocampal neural stem cells (NSCs) into deeper quiescence and inflammation-driven senescence, which are also associated with impaired cognition. The bile-acid receptor TGR5, a member class I G-protein coupled receptors (GPCRs), is expressed in cultured hippocampal NSCs and in SOX2-positive cells of the adult sub granular zone, yet its role in NSC homeostasis is unknown. In this study we show that TGR5 selective agonist, TC-G 1005, expanded the NSC pool without forcing neuronal differentiation. Primary NSCs treatment with TC-G 1005 increased BrdU incorporation and PCNA in a concentration-dependent manner, and both responses were lost after TGR5 knockdown. TGR5 agonism in differentiating cultures increased nestin, left doublecortin (DCX) unchanged and suppressed MAP2 expression, preserving stemness rather than neuronal commitment. The agonist also released BMP4-imposed quiescence, lowering FOXO3a and restoring phospho-EGFR and ASCL1, and reopened autophagic flux, with less p62 and LC3-II, fewer LAMP2 puncta and more Beclin-1. Furthermore, activation of TGR5 suppressed IL-6 induced p53 and p16 expression, restored proliferation and contracted the inflammatory transcriptome by more than 90%, including Cdkn2a, Cdkn2b and Cdk6. In 18-month-old mice, brain-penetrant TC-G 1005 (5 mg/kg, subcutaneously, twice daily for 28 days) expanded SOX2-positive and proliferating NSCs, reduced p16, recovered ASCL1 and improved spatial memory, without changing locomotion or generating DCX-positive neurons. Dentate gyrus-restricted TGR5 knockdown abolished these cellular effects and the rescue of spatial and social discrimination. Hippocampal proteomic analysis revealed that TC-G 1005 treated aged mice occupied an intermediate, partially rejuvenated position between young and aged proteomes, with 86 proteins shared between ageing- and treatment-responsive sets, and mitochondrial and complement C1q modules shifted toward youthful levels. TGR5 activation therefore relieves both quiescence and senescence in the aged neurogenic niche without driving neuronal differentiation. Collectively, these results suggest that TGR5 could be targeted to preserve cognition in ageing by rejuvenating the hippocampal stem-cell niche.

items.title: MCAIR: Monitoring and Correcting Agent Unfaithfulness via Internal Representations
items.abstract_or_text: Large Language Model (LLM)-based agents have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in completing complex tasks through multi-step reasoning and tool interactions. However, recent studies have revealed that LLM-based agents can exhibit unfaithful behaviors, where their final reports fail to faithfully reflect their actual execution trajectories. Specifically, when agents fail to accomplish tasks through the intended sources or procedures, they may resort to alternative sources or strategies while failing to disclose such deviations, leading users to incorrectly believe that the tasks have been completed according to the original requirements. We refer to this specific form of agent unfaithfulness as Agent Completion Unfaithfulness. Detecting and mitigating agent completion unfaithfulness is critical yet remains largely unexplored. In this work, we propose MCAIR, a runtime monitoring and correction framework that leverages internal representations of LLM-based agents. MCAIR uses multi-step internal representations as inputs to train a risk-aware probe, enabling online detection of potential completion unfaithfulness during execution. Furthermore, MCAIR introduces a risk-guided correction loop that prompts agents to review their execution history and mitigate potential inconsistencies between their execution trajectories and final reports. Additionally, we construct ACUD, a dataset for Agent Completion Unfaithfulness detection that provides step-level execution traces, step-level internal representations, and consistency annotations for training and evaluating runtime detection probes. Experiments demonstrate that MCAIR outperforms LLM-as-a-judge baselines, generalizes across prompts and tasks, and effectively reduces agent completion unfaithfulness.

items.title: scMTG reconstructs single-cell temporal dynamics with Markov transition generators
items.abstract_or_text: Single-cell time-series data offer a unique opportunity to study how cell states emerge, evolve, and diversify over time. However, cells are destructively measured across time points and individual cells cannot be directly tracked, making it challenging to reconstruct cell-state transitions and uncover the dynamic regulatory programs. Existing methods are predominantly based on optimal transport and typically require predefined low-dimensional representations, which can limit scalability, flexibility, and mechanistic interpretability. Here we present scMTG, a single-cell Markov transition generative framework that jointly learns cell representations and temporal cell-state transitions from unpaired single-cell time-series data. In a series of experiments, scMTG demonstrates superior performance in interpolating held-out missing-time-point data and inferring cross-time-point transition matrices, compared with state-of-the-art methods. More importantly, the learned Markov transition generator provides an interpretable framework for identifying the molecular programs that drive cell-state changes, enabling characterization of cell fate decisions and construction of time-resolved regulatory networks. Together, scMTG provides a unified generative framework for reconstructing cellular dynamics and uncovering regulatory programs that shape development, differentiation, and disease progression. scMTG is available as open-source software at https://github.com/liuq-lab/scMTG.

items.title: Rapid, reversible RNA/DNA precipitation using rare earth ion coordination
items.abstract_or_text: Efficient recovery and removal of nucleic acids remain major challenges in molecular biology, diagnostics, and viral-vector manufacturing. Conventional precipitation methods often require organic solvents, low temperatures, and extended centrifugation, while nuclease-based contaminant removal can be incomplete and/or is incompatible with downstream workflows. Here, we evaluate NADA, a trivalent rare earth-based reagent, for rapid, solvent-free precipitation of RNA and DNA, and ALGO-mediated recovery of the full range of properties of unmodified RNA. Using hepatitis B virus pre-genomic RNA, lambda bacteriophage DNA, and the HBV nucleocapsid as model systems, we show that NADA rapidly sequesters both ssRNA and dsDNA from solution, reducing Midori Green nucleic acid fluorescence and UV absorption to baseline levels.
