The NADA complex prevents HBV core protein binding to the HBV pgRNA, and therefore triggering of nucleocapsid formation, even when added simultaneously with core protein, suggesting that lanthanide ion coordination, out-competes the cognate Cp for viral RNA-binding interactions. Recovery with ALGO restores pgRNA integrity and functionality, enabling subsequent assembly of the expected T=4/T=3 nucleocapsids. In contrast, pre-assembled nucleocapsids resist NADA-ALGO treatment, demonstrating coat protein capsid-mediated protection of encapsidated pgRNA. Similar outcomes for lambda dsDNA establish NADA/ALGO as a rapid, reversible, and selective alternative platform for nucleic acid precipitation, with potential applications in viral particle purification, contaminant removal, and RNA handling workflows.

items.title: High-plex protein imaging across thick tissue by synchronized amplification
items.abstract_or_text: High-plex protein imaging is essential for decoding complex tissue organization, yet it remains largely confined to thin sections. Current approaches in millimeter-thick samples suffer from poor signal penetration and depth-dependent, uneven signal amplification. Even with specialized instrumentation to facilitate probe diffusion, iterative millimeter-thick tissue workflows can take more than four days per staining round, and reported eleven-marker experiments extend beyond a month. We introduce Amplification by Cyclic Extension (ACE), a DNA-barcoded, synchronized in situ amplification strategy that uses thermally controlled cyclic extension to coordinate DNA concatemer growth across tissue depths. By synchronously activating and coordinating reaction progression throughout the sample, ACE enables controlled, uniform signal amplification across tissue depths. Using ACE, we demonstrate 63-plex protein and RNA imaging in thin sections, 22-plex protein imaging in 200 m mouse brain sections, and 16-plex protein imaging in 1 mm-thick brain tissue encompassing over three million cells. For millimeter-thick tissues, ACE reduces per-round target-switching time from multiple days to less than eight hours, shifting volumetric high-plex protein imaging from months to days. Together, these results establish ACE as a synchronized amplification strategy that enables scalable high-plex protein imaging in thick tissues.

items.title: Verification Turns Capability Gaps into Routing Decisions: Small Language Models for Clinical Documentation
items.abstract_or_text: Clinical note generation from doctor--patient dialogue is high-volume and hallucination-intolerant: a fabricated laboratory value can create patient-safety risk, not a quality regression. We ask whether an agentic verification architecture, rather than generator scale, can make a small language model viable here. Holding a four-evaluator verification stack and refinement policy fixed and swapping only the generator between a 4B-parameter model with a QLoRA adapter and a frontier baseline, the small model reaches 0.984 claim-level factual entailment against 0.992 and comes within 3.3 points on completeness, generating entirely on-device. Its deficit is confined to inter-section structural fidelity---arrangement rather than clinical comprehension, and the axis on which it also falls furthest below the corpus's reference notes. Because that deficit is an explicit verifier decision rather than a silent quality difference, it becomes a routing policy: run the small model by default, escalate what the verifier rejects. Measured end to end, that it achieved a similiar verified-rate acceptance to the frontier-only acceptance in this test set (99.6\% vs.\ 98.4\% over 250 encounters) while routing 62, documenting three quarters without a frontier generation call. Ablating the loop separates architecture from scale: unrefined, the small model is accepted on 26.8\% of encounters and the frontier model on 74.8\%, so verification does the most work where the generator is weakest. We also contribute section-scoped refinement, which preserves unflagged sections by construction rather than instruction, and find the baseline is not uniformly stronger---its provider refused two trauma-related transcripts the on-device model handled and certified, one facet of a provider dependency a served adapter does not carry.

items.title: From Hindsight to Foresight: Dissecting Clinical Evidence Acquisition in Large Language Models
items.abstract_or_text: Large language models (LLMs) often diagnose full sight, static clinical cases well yet struggle in foresight, dynamic diagnosis. Prior work has improved this limitation by quantifying the information models acquire and by developing stronger follow-up strategies to improve diagnostic accuracy. In contrast, we introduce a distinctive hindsight to systematically dissect why LLMs fail to acquire diagnostically critical evidence, tracing the failure from evidence identification, utilization and downstream diagnostic updating through not only diagnostic accuracy, but also evidence coverage, trajectory dynamics, and elicited probability and information entropy. Starting experiments from the breakdown at the level of capabilities, to the diagnosis of the pre-event state before the evidence arrives, and to the post-event state transition after the evidence arrives, our research has revealed the profound limitations and internal causes existing in the dynamic diagnostic process. At the same time, we have also conducted sufficient verification and generalization experiments to prove that these limitations are widespread. Together, these findings shift the central challenge from whether LLMs possess relevant clinical knowledge to whether they can identify, acquire, and effectively use the right evidence under clinical diagnosis and conduct a more detailed mechanism analysis to identify the exact location of the capability gap.

items.title: The Last Mile of Coding Agents for Long-Document Tasks: An Empirical Study on Clinical Trial Protocol Digitization
items.abstract_or_text: Clinical trial protocols serve as the source of truth for study design, but are mostly written and used as unstructured PDF documents. Digitizing protocols turns static content into structured, machine-readable data that clinical software can analyze, validate, and execute. Coding agents, which select tools, execute code, and revise their approach as they work, are increasingly applied to such long-document tasks, yet it remains unclear how reliably they turn complete documents into accurate structured outputs. We study this question using protocol digitization as a testbed. We introduce TrialPD-Bench, an expert-annotated benchmark of 150 publicly available protocol PDFs spanning four task categories. Beyond final-answer performance, our evaluation measures evidence recall from agent traces, agent behavior, and cost. Across nine proprietary and open-weight models in five coding-agent harnesses, even the strongest agents do not fully solve protocol digitization. Our analysis further shows that agents usually locate the required evidence but fail in the last mile of transcribing and structuring it. We further develop TrialScribe, a domain-specific harness that equips coding agents with task skills and a verification loop. TrialScribe improves a locally served open-weight model by 6.2-59.4 points across eight metrics, enabling it to match or surpass proprietary models such as GPT-5.6-Sol.

items.title: Histone H2A.X contributes to Gene Expression Regulation and Cell-Cycle Progression in Toxoplasma gondii Tachyzoites
items.abstract_or_text: Histone H2A.X is a conserved variant classically associated with the DNA damage response (DDR), where its phosphorylation ({gamma}H2A.X) marks double-strand breaks and recruits repair factors. H2A.X is absent in many parasitic protozoans such as Plasmodium, Trypanosoma and Leishmania. In Toxoplasma gondii, the obligate intracellular parasite, causative agent of toxoplasmosis, however, its presence raises the question of whether it contributes to genome stability. To tackle this, we generated a T. gondii knockout of H2A.X (RH{Delta}H2A.X) and evaluated its phenotype. Although H2A.X is phosphorylated in response to DNA damage in T. gondii as in other systems, RH{Delta}H2A.X parasites showed no increased sensitivity to genotoxic agents, indicating that H2A.X is dispensable for canonical DDR. Instead, loss of H2A.X caused reduced gliding motility, increased host cell invasion and clustering of extracellular parasites after egress. Despite no defects in replication rate, RH{Delta}H2A.X showed delayed mitotic progression with abnormal vacuole morphology. Transcriptomic profiling revealed a moderate yet coordinated reprogramming of protein-coding genes. Specifically, H2A.X loss altered the expression of key apical secretory and virulence factors, especially ROP18, while inducing the transcriptional activation of mitotic and DNA replication machinery. Differential enrichment analysis further revealed that upregulated genes were preferentially associated with S phase, whereas downregulated genes were enriched during mitosis and cytokinesis. This is consistent with the delayed mitotic progression and spindle abnormalities observed by microscopy and flow cytometry and suggests a cell cycle phase-specific mechanism of H2A.X-dependent transcriptional control. Rather than a driver of DDR, these findings suggest that T. gondii H2A.X operates as a chromatin organizer that coordinates cell division fidelity and virulence gene expression.

items.title: Pan-cancer estimation of prognostic immune biomarkers from histopathology using artificial intelligence
items.abstract_or_text: Multiplex immunofluorescence (mIF) assays such as ImmunoProfile provide standardized quantification of prognostic immune markers but are costly and not routinely used in clinical settings. We developed a weakly-supervised AI model, HistoProfile, to estimate intratumoral cell densities of key immune biomarkers (CD8, FOXP3, PD-1, and PD-L1) and the PD-L1 tumor proportion score from routine H&E-stained whole-slide images. Trained on a large pan-cancer cohort with paired H&E and mIF data, HistoProfile discriminated biomarker-high from biomarker-low tumors in held-out samples and tumor-specific subgroups (AUROCs of 0.78-0.89 across biomarkers). Critically, the estimated biomarkers preserved prognostic stratification in downstream survival analyses, and showed cancer-specific survival associations across TCGA cohorts where mIF is unavailable. These findings support scalable H&E-based estimation of key immune biomarker measurements for large-scale immune profiling and risk stratification.

items.title: FERMAT: An Autoregressive Clinical Foundation Model for Disease Risk and Clinical Event Prediction
items.abstract_or_text: Clinical foundation models learn patterns in longitudinal health records that can be reused across prediction tasks. However, the relative strengths of representation-based and generation-based prediction across clinical tasks remain unclear. Using longitudinal electronic health records from 3.77 million patients at a single hospital, we developed FERMAT (Foundation model for Exploring Real-world Multimodal health data using Autoregressive Trajectory modeling), a 65-million-parameter clinical foundation model. We compared predictions from task-specific predictors trained on patient representations with those derived from generated clinical event sequences. Representation-based prediction performed better in the disease-risk comparisons. In detailed analyses of five-year chronic kidney disease, fatty liver, and diabetes risk in a test cohort of 10,000 patients, representation-based predictors exceeded generation-based estimates by 0.098-0.115 in observation-weighted AUROC and had lower probability error. Generation-based prediction, in turn, performed better in predicting diagnoses, prescriptions, and procedures recorded on the same day, a task motivated by the frequent presence of multiple events with the same date in hospital EHRs. Using 50 generated trajectories per patient, it achieved a Recall@10 of 71.0%, compared with 55.7% for representation-based prediction, with a paired improvement of 15.31 percentage points (95% CI, 13.92-16.79; n = 1,862). These findings demonstrate task-dependent strengths of representation-based and generation-based applications within a single clinical foundation model, providing an empirical basis for exploring how the two approaches can be used individually or combined to address clinical prediction needs.

items.title: Foundation Model Artificial Intelligence for Electrocardiogram Detection of Rheumatic Mitral Stenosis
items.abstract_or_text: Background: Rheumatic mitral stenosis (RMS) disproportionately affects low-resource settings where echocardiography is limited. We evaluated foundation model (FM) feasibility for RMS detection using limited, indirectly labeled ECGs. Methods: An ECG-FM was fine-tuned using 804 RMS-positive ECGs per fold and externally validated across clinical and wearable lead configurations. Results: Internal AUROCs were 0.89, 0.87, and 0.87, for 12-Lead, 6-Lead, and 1-Lead respectively. External AUROCs were 0.82, 0.80, and 0.77. Performance remained comparable across demographic subgroups. Conclusions: FM fine-tuning enables RMS detection using limited ICD-derived labels, supporting further evaluation of reduced-lead ECG screening and echocardiography triage in resource-constrained settings.

items.title: Cortex-wide single-cell activity mapping in freely moving mice
items.abstract_or_text: How the cortex supports complex, naturalistic behavior can be revealed only in freely moving animals. Although head-mounted microscopes promise access to the neural dynamics underlying such behavior, fundamental trade-offs among field of view, spatial resolution, device weight, and background contamination have prevented cortex-wide single-neuron recording, leaving distributed cortical coordination largely inaccessible. To meet these challenges, we introduce COMET (Cortex-wide Observational Miniature Epifluorescence Technique), a 3.75-g head-mounted mesoscope that integrates an aberration-controlled wide-field optical design, uniform high-efficiency excitation and single-coaxial power-and-data transmission with an end-to-end denoising and signal-extraction pipeline. This enables cortex-wide calcium imaging at single-cell resolution in freely moving mice. COMET captures activity from >15,000 layer 2/3 neurons per 5-min recording over fields of view up to 10 mm in diameter while preserving natural behavior. Benchmarking against benchtop two-photon microscopy demonstrates high spatial concordance of detected neurons and matched event-level calcium dynamics. We apply COMET to social interaction to quantify region-specific engagement and to an auditory trace fear-conditioning task that requires natural movement and behavioral expression, revealing time-ordered changes in regional firing-rate structure and functional connectivity preceding a global conditioned response. COMET provides an open, lightweight hardware-software framework for linking single-neuron activity to cortex-scale network dynamics during freely expressed behaviors under changing internal or external conditions.

items.title: Diagnostic accuracy of deep learning for microsatellite instability prediction in gastric cancer: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.abstract_or_text: Deep learning (DL) applied to haematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-stained pathology images can predict microsatellite instability (MSI) in gastric cancer (GC). We evaluated its diagnostic accuracy and discriminative performance. PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library and Web of Science were searched for studies applying DL to H&E images for MSI prediction in GC. The protocol was prospectively registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261503140). Risk of bias was assessed with QUADAS-2. Pooled sensitivity and specificity were estimated with a bivariate random-effects model, with subgroup analyses by validation strategy and data source; slide-level areas under the curve (AUCs) were pooled after logit transformation. Prespecified scenario analyses assessed robustness. Ten studies were included; seven independent datasets from six studies entered the primary synthesis. Pooled sensitivity, specificity and summary receiver operating characteristic AUC were 0.78 (95% CI 0.63-0.88), 0.85 (95% CI 0.77-0.90) and 0.89 (95% CI 0.86-0.91); nine studies contributed to the secondary AUC synthesis (pooled AUC 0.85, 95% CI 0.80-0.89). Hospital-derived cohorts showed numerically higher sensitivity (0.86) and diagnostic odds ratio (39.8) than TCGA-derived cohorts (0.71 and 11.5), but subgroup differences were limited by the small number of studies and substantial heterogeneity. DL models show good diagnostic accuracy for MSI prediction in GC, but clinical utility still requires confirmation in standardised multicentre, independent external and prospective studies.

items.title: AgentSafeEvo: Adversarial Co-Evolution for LLM Agent Safety
items.abstract_or_text: Large language model (LLM) agents accomplish complex tasks through multi-turn interactions with external tools. However, malicious content embedded in user queries, tool descriptions, or environment observations can manipulate their decisions and induce unsafe actions. Adversarial co-evolution has emerged as an effective approach to strengthening LLM safety, but existing work primarily focuses on language-level safety or indirect prompt injection in web tasks. In this paper, we introduce AgentSafeEvo, a co-evolutionary reinforcement learning framework for agent safety built on an attacker-defender game spanning diverse tasks and attack types. The attacker learns to construct adversarial agent tasks that expose weaknesses in the defender's tool use, while the defender learns to complete tasks safely under these attacks. We further introduce learnability-guided task weighting, which uses within-task defender-reward variability to adjust each task's contribution to attacker and defender updates. Extensive experiments on agent safety and general capability benchmarks demonstrate that our method improves adversarial robustness while maintaining general agent capabilities.

items.title: Progerin disrupts intestinal epithelial homeostasis by impairing mitochondrial metabolism and absorptive enterocyte maturation
items.abstract_or_text: Hutchinson-Gilford progeria syndrome (HGPS) is a segmental premature ageing disease that predominantly affects tissues with high regenerative capacity. Although the intestine is the most rapidly self-renewing tissue of adult mammals, it has so far been considered only as a source of microbiota-derived disturbances in progeria, and whether the intestinal epithelium is itself a target of progerin remains unknown. Here, using the LmnaG609G/G609G and LmnaG609G/+ mouse models, intestinal organoids and single-cell RNA sequencing, we show that progerin is expressed in colonic enterocytes and in SMA+ subepithelial myofibroblasts of the stem-cell niche. Heterozygous progeria mice develop increased intestinal permeability from 30 weeks of age, reaching levels reported in physiologically aged (>20-month-old) mice. Progeria-derived intestinal organoids display reduced mitochondrial oxygen consumption, a compensatory increase in glycolysis and impaired crypt budding. Single-cell transcriptomics of the colonic epithelium and lamina propria revealed that, while lineage composition is preserved, progerin induces a coordinated reprogramming characterised by repression of oxidative phosphorylation and mitochondrial quality-control genes, including Nod2, activation of interferon, TNF-NF-kB and innate defence programs, and up-regulation of RNA-processing and chromatin-associated pathways. Trajectory analysis showed that progeria absorptive enterocytes selectively fail to reach terminal differentiation states and retain progenitor-like WNT, NOTCH and EGFR signatures, while lacking the mitochondrial programs required for maturation. Together, these findings identify the intestinal epithelium as a cell-intrinsic target of progerin and support a model in which mitochondrial insufficiency stalls absorptive enterocyte maturation and weakens the intestinal barrier, recapitulating, prematurely, key features of colon ageing.

items.title: Preemptive SOD1 Silencing via Neonatal Intramuscular AAV Therapy Modifies Disease Trajectory in an ALS Mouse Model
items.abstract_or_text: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a progressive and fatal neurodegenerative disorder with limited therapeutic options. Mutations in the gene encoding superoxide dismutase 1 (SOD1) represent a major genetic cause of familial ALS, driving motor neuron degeneration through toxic gain-of-function mechanisms. Although gene silencing approaches targeting SOD1 show substantial therapeutic potential, their clinical translation remains restricted by suboptimal delivery to the spinal motor neurons and safety concerns linked to conventional viral vectors. This study presents a minimally invasive gene therapy strategy that combines the retrograde transport capability of rAAV2-retro with the safety of an artificial microRNA (miRNA) to achieve pan-spinal SOD1 silencing. A single intramuscular injection of rAAV2-retro-miRNA into neonatal SOD1G93A mice resulted in widespread transduction of spinal motor neurons, significant reduction of mutant SOD1 protein, and multifaceted therapeutic benefits. Treated mice exhibited delayed disease onset, extended lifespan, preserved motor function, reduced neuroinflammation, and protection of neuromuscular junctions and spinal motor neurons. Importantly, the artificial miRNA construct demonstrated a superior safety profile relative to short hairpin RNA (shRNA)-based constructs, which induced marked toxicity and lethality in wild-type mice. These findings establish neonatal intramuscular delivery of rAAV2-retro-miRNA as a safe, efficient, and clinically translatable strategy for preemptive intervention in SOD1-mediated ALS, offering broader applicability to other motor neuron diseases.

items.title: Deep learning-based virtual perturbation reveals increasing heterogeneity of gene regulatory responses with aging
items.abstract_or_text: A central hypothesis in aging biology proposes that the gradual accumulation of stochastic molecular damage drives transcriptional deregulation (TD), ultimately leading to functional decline. However, existing single-cell analyses largely rely on static expression measurements and provide limited resolution of how regulatory responses change at the level of individual cells. Here, we leverage DKO, a deep learning framework that predicts cell-specific virtual gene perturbation effects from unperturbed transcriptomes, capturing cell-to-cell differences in regulatory context without requiring a reconstructed gene regulatory network or matched perturbation data. Applying DKO to single-cell transcriptomic datasets from humans, mice, Drosophila, and C. elegans revealed that the transcriptional consequences of perturbing the same gene became increasingly heterogeneous across cells with age, indicating that gene regulatory responses become less consistent and more dependent on cellular context. Furthermore, we find that cells with higher somatic mutation burdens have greater knockout-response variability, linking accumulated molecular damage to regulatory inconsistency. Within the same cellular populations, higher impact variability was also associated with higher senescence scores, linking transcriptional dysregulation to senescence-associated states. Our findings identify a progressive loss of regulatory robustness at both the gene and cell levels as a conserved feature of aging, linking stochastic molecular damage to increasing heterogeneity in cellular regulatory responses.

items.title: SMI: Ontology-Grounded Semantic IDs for Hierarchy-Aware Medical Concept Representation
items.abstract_or_text: Biomedical language models (LMs) provide strong representations for clinical tasks, but they often fail to capture the hierarchical structure among medical concepts. This limitation is especially pronounced for rare and fine-grained clinical codes in long-tailed vocabularies, where hierarchy-agnostic LM representations become less informative as concept frequency decreases. We introduce Semantic Medical Identifier (SMI), a training-free framework for constructing ontology-grounded Semantic IDs and hierarchy-aware medical concept representations. For each diagnosis, procedure, or medication concept, SMI defines its Semantic ID as the coarse-to-fine path through an expert-defined medical ontology. SMI then aggregates frozen biomedical LM embeddings across the corresponding ontology levels to form hierarchy-aware medical concept representations that preserve coarse-to-fine clinical semantics. The base SMI uses uniform aggregation across ontology levels, while a level-weighted variant selects global level weights on validation data. Our theoretical analysis shows that SMI yields more informative medical concept representations than hierarchy-agnostic LM embeddings, particularly for rare and fine-grained clinical concepts. Experiments show that SMI captures meaningful hierarchical structure and improves clinical relation prediction. On MIMIC-IV, SMI improves mortality prediction, readmission prediction, drug recommendation, and rare drug prediction. On eICU, SMI yields more robust patient representations under cross-hospital distribution shift.

items.title: RT-J: Large-Scale Pretraining of Relational Transformers for Context-Efficient Predictions
items.abstract_or_text: Foundation models for tables and relational databases are increasingly used for predictive tasks across various scientific and industrial domains. However, adapting existing models to unseen datasets requires tens of thousands of examples. Here we introduce RT-J, an 85M-parameter relational foundation model (RFM) that makes accurate predictions even with hundreds of in-context examples or fewer. To achieve this, we first assemble the Join, a large collection of 639 web-crawled databases with 6,023 LLM-generated forecasting tasks. We pretrain with long contexts of up to 8,192 database cells, using in-context examples from a novel lightweight random-walk retriever. Finally, we leverage context tuning and ensembling to scale up test-time compute. On in-context regression tasks from RelBench, RT-J requires 10x fewer examples on average to match strong feature engineering pipelines with LLM-agent or RDBLearn featurizers and TabICLv2 or LightGBM predictors. Overall, our work pushes the frontier for context-efficient predictions on relational data and highlights the importance of real-world semantics, context engineering and large-scale pretraining for RFMs.

items.title: Why Static Skill Inconsistencies Do Not Equate to Runtime Risks: A Behavioral Analysis of LLM Agent Execution
items.abstract_or_text: LLM agent frameworks heavily rely on external skill assets to standardize tool usage, encode operational workflows, and supply executable runtime resources. Despite their widespread adoption, multi-component skill packages frequently suffer from cross-artifact inconsistencies, where documentation, scripts, and configuration files specify conflicting behavioral constraints. Although static auditing techniques can uncover such contractual discrepancies, static defect volume cannot reliably reflect real-world agent performance degradation. This gap leaves practitioners without rigorous evidence to assess the practical risk of flawed agent skills. This paper presents a systematic empirical study to demystify the runtime implications of skill inconsistencies. We conduct large-scale auditing over 575 community and benchmark skills, yielding 1,182 manually validated contract inconsistencies. We further build a controlled evaluation pipeline with 49 executable agent tasks and three representative LLMs across NoSkill, OriginalSkill, and FixedSkill experimental settings. Through fine-grained behavioral analysis of 441 paired execution trajectories, we quantify the actual performance impacts of resolved defects.
